title: Dasharatha's arrow
hookLine: a young prince shoots at a sound in the dark, and the deed ripens decades later: karma, the storehouse of action
carry: karma: every deed is a seed that ripens
tomorrow: a king gets a thousand years of youth. is it enough?
last: ABHINIVESHA: EVEN THE WISE CLING TO LIFE.

lines: A SHOT AT A SOUND IN THE DARK.
cards: Long before Rama is born, his father Dasharatha is a young prince with a well-known skill: he can hit a target by sound alone. One night by the Sarayu river he hears a gurgling at the water's edge.
An elephant drinking, he thinks, and he shoots. A cry comes back, a human cry. He runs down and finds a young ascetic, his water pot in the river, an arrow in his side.
The boy's parents are old and blind, waiting for that water.

teach.h: 'YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.'
teach.b: The boy, whom later tellings call Shravan, asks the prince to go to his father, and dies. Dasharatha carries the water to the old couple and confesses. The father, in his grief, says: you too will die grieving for a son.
Decades pass. Dasharatha becomes a great king.

Then Rama is sent into exile, and on the night Dasharatha dies of that grief, the Ramayana has him remember the river and tell his queen: whatever a person does, good or bad, the doer reaps its fruit.
That is karma, one of Hinduism's central teachings. Patanjali gives its workings.
Sutra 2.12: karmashaya, the storehouse of action. Every deed leaves a deposit, rooted in the afflictions, lived out in this birth or one unseen.
Sutra 2.13: while that root is there, it ripens three ways, as a birth, a life span and what is lived through. And 2.14: joy from merit, pain from its opposite. There's no scorekeeper in the sutras.
It's closer to farming: seed, soil, time.
The commentary adds hope: rice in its husk can sprout, but husked or roasted, it won't. The afflictions are the husk; thin them by practice and old seeds lose their power.
And notice who names Dasharatha's deed: Dasharatha. Many teachers say karma is for reading your own actions, not for judging someone else's pain.
Today the storehouse fills quietly: the sharp text, the patient answer, the help nobody saw. Each one a seed.

how: Dasharatha's memory of the boy at the river, from the Ramayana, is one of the best-known Hindu tellings of a deed's fruit returning; later tellings name the boy Shravan Kumar and honor his care for his blind parents. Teachers of the Yoga Sutras present practice as the way to weaken the afflictions that make stored action sprout.

games.q: a friend says karma means anyone who suffers must have deserved it. what fits the sutras and Dasharatha's story?
o: yes: point at people's pain and name their karma.
Dasharatha read his own deed. many teachers say karma is for your own actions, and practice thins the root.
karma is just luck; deeds leave nothing behind.
games.why: nobody accuses Dasharatha; he names the seed himself. and 2.13 says seeds ripen only while the root remains, so practice on the husk matters.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you did yesterday, kind or unkind, and notice what it left in you: a warmth, a tightness, a replay.
That's the deposit; just see it clearly, the way you'd hold a seed in your palm, without judging or fixing it. Then set it down and come back to the breath, which is happening now, not yesterday.

wordCard.voice: Karmashaya, the storehouse of action. Every deed leaves a deposit there, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and an experience.

orig.note: Sanskrit karmāśaya: karma (action) plus āśaya (resting place, receptacle), the storehouse of action.

carryVoice: Your line: karma, every deed is a seed that ripens. Dasharatha's arrow came back to him. Day four hundred fifty-three, done.
